text: Right, everyone gets a job, so nobody can say the crown played favourites. Graham, you hold the Harvest Pile, since wheat people count carefully. Paddy, you collect the tax, and please be gentle with your neighbours. Silke, you read the I Ching, and the crown pays you five a year to tell us honestly what the heavens say.

Reina appoints her table jobs for the whole game: Graham Garner banks the Harvest Pile and pays out every harvest, Paddy Doyle collects the tax, and Silke Weber reads the I Ching card each year and keeps the population counter, for 5 a year from the crown. Silke shuffles the I Ching deck.

Storyteller's tip: every work owed at this table is the crown's to pay for, 520 in all. That's eight projects (the three palaces, the Wall above Province 1, the canals in Provinces 1, 5 and 6, and the Province 7 Reservoir), and only one can be built a year. Tax can be raised only on positive incomes.

Forty percent this year, friends. That's twenty-four from each of you, and you still keep more than you hand over. The crown pays for the Summer Palace on its own, and next year we start on the Wall and the canals.

Paddy collects the tax at 40%: 24 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 72 to the crown. Reina builds the Summer Palace on G20 in Province 1, paying the 20 herself; the Wall above Province 1 and the Province 1 canal can now be built. 500 of the works are still owed.

Thank you, Your Majesty. Five a year to read the heavens is fair, and I'll read them honestly, good news or bad. The Dragon Jar goes up first, opening at four. It's a lovely piece, and nobody at this table has much money, so I'm not going to pretend it's worth forty.

Thank you, Reina, I'll be gentle with the collecting, I promise. Right then, one Bamboo Brush from the rice country, starting at four. It's a good honest brush, and I've got another just like it for next year, so nobody needs to go mad over it.
One Land Deed Scroll, opening at two. I've got two of them, so whoever wants paper on the land had better start now.

This year's lots: Silke puts up the Dragon Jar (the only one in the game), minimum 4; Paddy puts up one of his two Bamboo Brushes, minimum 4; Graham puts up one of his two Land Deed Scrolls, minimum 2.
Paddy's and Graham's sets both need the Dragon Jar, and it's the only one in the game.

Well, I was wrong about the Dragon Jar. Paddy, Graham, it turns out you both need it and there's only the one, so it opens at four and the two of you can sort it out between you. I'll take a polite interest in the brush and the scroll, and I won't be emptying my purse on either.

Graham, I won't pretend I don't want that Jar, because I do, and so do you. If we fight over it, the Harvest Pile gets fat and we both go hungry. Still, there's only the one, so I'll bid what's sensible. Brush stays at four.

Only one Dragon Jar in the whole game, so I'll bid on it, and I won't be shy about it. Paddy, you've got two brushes. If one ends up in Silke's hands this year, that's fine by me, there's another one next spring.

The auctions: Paddy wins the Dragon Jar for 17 over Graham's 16; Silke keeps 4 of it. Silke wins the Bamboo Brush for 5 over Graham's 4, and the Land Deed Scroll for 6: Paddy's limit was also 6, and a tie goes to the earlier seat.

Seventeen. That's more grain than I like to spend on anything I can't eat, but there was only the one. Sorry, Graham, you pushed me right to the edge there. She goes in the middle of the paddies where I can keep an eye on her.
A brush and a deed for eleven, and four back from my Jar. Thank you, gentlemen. Paddy, enjoy the Jar. Seventeen is a lot of rice to hand over for one pot.
Only the winner pays at an auction: Paddy paid 17 for the Dragon Jar, and Graham paid nothing.

Paddy puts the Dragon Jar on R22. Silke puts the Bamboo Brush on P25 and the Land Deed Scroll on P26. Reina pays Silke her 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 1: Reina 107, Silke 34, Paddy 20, Graham 37.5; Harvest Pile 2301.5.

The heavens say: 'The Canal Gives Way. The engineers blame the river. The river declines to comment.' Average harvest in every province. Any unfinished Grand Canal work is lost, and since nobody has dug a canal yet, the crown loses nothing. Provinces 2, 3, 7 and 8 play a Personal Disaster, so Graham, I'm sorry, but that's you. The population holds at one hundred million, times one, so read the first row of your tables.
Graham pays out an average harvest from the Harvest Pile: +35 each to Silke, Paddy and Graham, +15 to Reina. Graham's disaster #1: a late frost blackens the edge of the wheat, 2 to the Harvest Pile.

Forty percent again, which comes to fourteen each on a thin year. Graham, I'm sorry about the frost. The crown digs the whole northern canal this year, both sections in one go, so the river has nothing half-finished to swallow. Your Reservoir is on the list, and it's coming.

Paddy collects the tax at 40%: 14 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 42 to the crown. Reina digs both sections of the Grand Canal in Province 1, paying the 80 herself; they add 20 to her harvest from next year. 420 of the works are still owed.
Second brush, as promised, Graham, same as the first, opening at four. And I'm sorry about the frost. Losing two to a cold night is hard on anybody.
The other Land Deed Scroll. Minimum five. Paddy, you went to six for the last one.

This year's lots: Silke puts up one of her two Customs Houses (her only type left; she sets its minimum in her bids); Paddy puts up his second Bamboo Brush, minimum 4; Graham puts up his last Land Deed Scroll, minimum 5.
One Customs House, opening at three. It's good for trade and a quiet port. As for the brush and the scroll, I already have mine, gentlemen, so I'm only watching. Mostly.

Graham, there are two Customs Houses and two of us after them. Let's not feed the Harvest Pile. You take this one, I'll only put in a small bid, and next year you leave the second one to me. That's fair, isn't it? And yes, I'll be bidding on that last scroll, I won't pretend otherwise.

Paddy. Silke has two Customs Houses, and you and I need one each. I won't bid against you on this one if you leave the next one to me. No point feeding the Pile." (A pause.) "The brush I'll take at Paddy's price.

The auctions: Graham wins the Customs House for 5 over Paddy's 4; Silke keeps 1. Silke wins the last Bamboo Brush for 6 over Graham's 5; Paddy keeps 1.5. Paddy wins the last Land Deed Scroll for 13 over Silke's 12; Graham keeps 3.
Q15. Thank you, Paddy, the next one's yours, as agreed." (Quietly.) "Silke. You already had a brush.
Two brushes on my coast, so I'll be the best-lettered peasant in China. Graham, I'm sorry, but six is cheap for a good brush, and you agreed it was Paddy's price.

Thirteen, and Silke, you made me earn every grain of it, for a scroll you already had. Graham, we crossed our wires on who got which Customs House, but you've got this one now, so by my reckoning the last one's mine next year and you'll stand aside. I'll hold you to that, same as I'd hold myself.
Graham puts the Customs House on Q15, Silke her second Bamboo Brush on P24, Paddy the Land Deed Scroll on R23 beside his Jar. Reina pays Silke her 5 for reading the I Ching.

End of Year 2. Grain: Reina 79, Silke 55, Paddy 29.5, Graham 54.5; Harvest Pile 2282. Built: the Summer Palace and both Province 1 canal sections (+20 to Reina's harvest from Year 3); 420 of the works still owed. Held: Silke 2 Bamboo Brushes and a Land Deed Scroll (needs the Wooden Bowl and the Vase); Paddy the Dragon Jar and a Scroll (needs a Customs House and the Vase); Graham a Customs House (needs a Brush, the Dragon Jar and the Wooden Bowl). Still beside the board: Silke 1 Customs House, Paddy the Wooden Bowl, Graham the Vase.

Population Grows by Half. The villages are noisier than they used to be." Good harvest everywhere, no disasters named. The counter goes to 150 million, so that's times one and a half, everyone. Read the x1.5 row, and remember your mouths just got hungrier too. Honest reading, as promised.
Graham pays out a good harvest from the Harvest Pile at x1.5: +40 each to Silke, Paddy and Graham (100 less 60 eaten), +30 to Reina (100 and the Province 1 canal's 20, less 90 eaten).

A good year, and a good year is when the crown asks for more. Fifty percent, which is twenty a head, and you each still clear twenty. Graham, I said the Reservoir was coming, and it's coming now. The crown puts in forty if you put in twenty, and it pays you twenty a year from next harvest, so your share is back in your pocket after one year. Silke, your five, as always.

Paddy collects the tax at 50%: 20 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 60 to the crown. Reina proposes the Province 7 Reservoir (60, +20 a year to Province 7's harvest from next year): the crown pays 40 if Graham pays 20. The Reservoir is the crown's work, so Graham's share is his choice.
Twenty in, twenty back each year from next harvest. That pays for itself in one year, Reina, and I don't argue with a number like that. Build it.

Reina and Graham build the Province 7 Reservoir on O16 to P17, the crown paying 40 and Graham 20, into the Harvest Pile. It adds 20 to Graham's harvest from next year. 360 of the works are still owed.
I said I'd stand aside on the Customs House, so I'm standing aside. Paddy, it's yours to win. The Bowl I'll bid on, and the Vase opens at eight. There's only one, and two of you need it.

Graham and I shook on this Customs House last year, and I'm grateful he's keeping to it. Silke, I'll not pretend I don't want your Vase too, Graham, so I'll bid it honestly and no higher than I can stand. And the Bowl goes up at four. It's a good bowl, and I'll not give it away.
My last Customs House starts at fifteen, Paddy. It's the only one left in China, and you know exactly what it's worth to you. As for the pottery, I'm only bidding to keep the kiln-men honest.

The auctions. Silke's last Customs House opens at 15; Paddy, the only bidder, would go to 8, so it goes unsold: it stays beside the board and must go up again next year at 2. Silke wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 13 over Graham's 12 (Paddy keeps 3), and Graham's Vase for 25 over Paddy's 24 (Graham keeps 6).
A bowl and a vase on the coast, next to my brushes and my deed. Thank you, Paddy, and thank you, Graham, both very fair prices. I'm only putting them on the shelf. For now.

Silke puts the Wooden Bowl on P23 and the Vase on P22. She now holds a complete set (Bamboo Brush, Land Deed Scroll, Wooden Bowl, Vase) and 37 grain, more than the 20 she must keep, so she may change seats: with no upper class at this table, the Silk Peasant may take the throne.

Brush, scroll, bowl and vase, and grain to spare. Reina, the cards have been reading honestly all along, and this year they say the Mandate moves to the coast. I take the throne. Don't worry, the I Ching still needs a reader, and I'll pay a fair five for one.

Silke declares her set and takes the throne. Silke is now the Emperor, in Province 1, with the crown's reserve: 166. Reina is now the Silk Peasant, in Province 5, and draws 60 from the Harvest Pile. A new Emperor returns every piece: both Bamboo Brushes and the Wooden Bowl go back to Paddy's stock, the Land Deed Scroll and the Vase to Graham's, to be auctioned again. The unsold Customs House stays in Province 5's stock, now Reina's to sell, and must go up next year at 2. Still beside the board: Province 5 (Reina) 1 Customs House; Province 6 (Paddy) 2 Bamboo Brushes, 1 Wooden Bowl; Province 7 (Graham) 1 Land Deed Scroll, 1 Vase.

Graham keeps the Harvest Pile and takes the cards, at five a year, the same as I got. Paddy keeps the tax. Reina, rest those hands for a year, you've earned it. I'll run an honest crown, but not a soft one.

Silke, as Emperor, keeps Graham on the Harvest Pile and gives him the I Ching and the population counter too, at 5 a year, paid now; Paddy keeps collecting the tax; Reina holds no job. End of Year 3: Silke (the crown) 161, Reina 60, Paddy 52.5, Graham 65.5.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." The counter stays at 150 million, so it's still times one and a half, everyone. Read the bad-harvest row at x1.5. No disasters named. And Your Majesty, a bad year is a poor year for fifty percent.

Graham pays out a bad harvest at x1.5. Reina and Paddy each lose 10 (50 less 60 eaten), paid into the Harvest Pile; Graham gains 10 (50 and the Reservoir's 20, less 60); Silke, as Emperor, loses 20 (50 and the Province 1 canal's 20, less 90). Only Graham's income is positive, so only Graham owes tax this year (Note 8).

Graham's right, a rotten year is no year to squeeze anyone. Thirty percent, and only Graham owes it, three grain. The crown pays for the Winter Palace itself, and that opens the way for canals on the coast, Reina's and Paddy's.

Paddy collects the tax at 30%: 3 from Graham, the only positive income, to the crown. Silke builds the Winter Palace on H21 in Province 1, paying the 20 herself, into the Harvest Pile; the canals in Provinces 5 and 6 can now be built. 340 of the works are still owed.

The Bowl's come home to me again, so up it goes. Six to start. Graham went to twelve for it last year, so I don't think six is asking much. And Reina, I'm sorry about the throne. That Customs House of yours at two is the first good news I've had in a year.
The Vase again. It's still the only one in China, and last year it went for twenty-five. It opens at ten.

This year's lots: Reina's Customs House, unsold last year, must go up again at 2; Paddy puts up the Wooden Bowl, minimum 6, and keeps both Bamboo Brushes back; Graham puts up the Vase, minimum 10, and keeps the Land Deed Scroll back.

Well. Silke played the long game and played it beautifully, and I'll say so on the record. The coast is mine now, so I'm starting over like everyone else: my Customs House is up at two, cheap, and I'll be bidding on the pottery, but nobody's going to see me burn my grain to get it.

Reina, I'll take that Customs House off your hands, and gladly. Graham, ten's a fair start for the Vase. I'll say it plainly to everyone: if I get the House and the Vase both, I've got my set, and I'll still have my twenty grain kept by.
The Customs House is Paddy's business, not mine. I'll bid for the Bowl, though, because I need it, and I won't lose it by one grain twice.
Paddy, you told the whole table that the Vase finishes your set, and I've just come off the throne, so I know exactly what that sentence means. Sorry, the Vase is coming to the coast.
Twenty-two and a half, and that's every grain I can spare and still keep my twenty. I won't pretend I've got more, Reina. If you go past it, it's yours, and I'll shake your hand.

The auctions settle. Paddy wins Reina's Customs House for 2, unopposed (Reina keeps 0.5). Graham wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 9 over Reina's 8 (Paddy keeps 2). The Vase was close, so Reina and Paddy each had one raise: Reina to 26, Paddy to 22.5. Reina wins the Vase for 23.5 (Graham keeps 5.5).
Right next to the Deed, there. Well played, Reina, I said I'd shake your hand and I will. But the Vase only has to come back round once, and when it does, I'll be the one waiting for it.
Nine. I lost by one grain last year, so it's a pleasure to win by one this time. It goes next to my Customs House. Paddy, those two brushes in your stock: I'll be bidding on one when it comes up.
Back on the shelf where Silke had it, P22. Paddy, I'll take that handshake, and I mean it. You bid honestly and you stopped where you said you'd stop.

Paddy puts the Customs House on R24, beside his Scroll and Jar; Graham puts the Wooden Bowl on Q16, beside his Customs House; Reina puts the Vase on P22. Silke pays Graham 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 4: Silke (the crown) 119, Reina 27, Paddy 42.5, Graham 74; Harvest Pile 2237.5. 340 of the works are still owed.

Population Grows by Half." It has already grown by half once, so that part doesn't count. Only the good harvest does. The counter stays at 150 million, times one and a half. Everyone reads the good-harvest column on the x1.5 row. Nobody plays a disaster this year.

A good harvest is a good year for everyone, the throne included. Forty percent, and in return the capital gets a Pagoda you can see from the coast. Reina, Paddy, look out your windows: that's your tax standing up in marble.

The auctions. Paddy and Graham each hold only one type beside the board: Paddy puts up a Bamboo Brush and Graham the Land Deed Scroll, each at a minimum they name in their bids. Reina has nothing left in stock. The Emperor doesn't bid.

Forty in a good year, Silke, and a Pagoda besides. I'll take that, and I'll hold you to the coast canal next. Graham, nobody else at this table needs that scroll, so let's not feed the Harvest Pile for nothing: open it at the minimum and it's mine for a few grain. Paddy, you've got two brushes, so there's one for each of us if Graham and I don't drive the first one up.
Just the one Bamboo Brush from me, at two, and somebody's welcome to it. The Deed's no use to me, I've got one already on my paddies, so I'll keep my hands in my pockets for that one, Graham.

There are two brushes, Reina, so neither of us has to bleed for the first one. I'll go to a fair price and stop there. The Scroll opens at six. That's less than I paid to stand aside for Paddy's Customs House.
The auctions. Paddy's Bamboo Brush, minimum 2: Graham wins it for 13 over Reina's 12 (Paddy keeps 3). Graham's Land Deed Scroll, minimum 6: Reina, the only bidder, takes it for 6 (Graham keeps 1.5).
Thirteen, one more than you, Reina. Paddy still has a brush in his stock, and it'll come cheaper than mine did. Enjoy the Scroll.
Thank you, Graham. Six was a fair opening and I won't forget it. The deed goes next to the Vase, so the coast has two pieces now. Enjoy the brush, and save the second one for me, Paddy.

Graham places the Bamboo Brush on Q17 and Reina the Land Deed Scroll on P23. Silke pays Graham 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 5: Silke (the crown) 180, Reina 45, Paddy 69.5, Graham 103.5. Still beside the board: Paddy 1 Bamboo Brush.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families." A good harvest in every province, but the counter goes to 300 million. That's times three now, so read the times-three row. Everyone's consumption doubles from here. Feed them while you still can.
Graham pays out the good harvest at x3: Silke -60, Reina -20, Paddy -20, Graham 0. Every negative income is paid into the pile, so nobody has a taxable income this year.

Storyteller's tip: every province's square needs some share from the crown, even 1 grain a square, so a crown in debt stops all new land at the table, its own included. Your board card shows how many squares Province 1 needs to break even, and a bad harvest is 25 below an average one.

Three hundred million mouths, and not one province with a grain of income to tax. So no marble this year. Every grain the crown has goes into the ground. I'll pay five on every square any of you buys, and I'm buying four for the north myself. Fill your fields first, then come and ask me for canals. Reina, the coast canal is still coming. It comes once there's a harvest to pay for it.

Tax 40% raises nothing: no province has a positive income. Silke builds nothing this year. Province 1 buys four squares of sea, F23 to F26, for 80, so the crown's reserve is 40. The crown offers 5 on every square a province buys this year.

Storyteller's tip: a square bought this year starts yielding with next year's harvest and pays for itself in a year. Your board card shows how many you need to break even, now and after the next card. A player in debt can't buy any.

Silke, five a square is a kind offer to someone who has the grain. I have twenty-five. Here's every grain I can put in the ground, twenty for two squares, and I'm asking the crown to match it, ten a square. Three hundred million mouths on the coast is your problem as much as mine, and an empty coast doesn't pay for canals.

Eight a square, Reina. That's sixteen from the crown and twenty-four from you, and you've got twenty-five, so both squares go in the ground. I'm not tipping my last grain into the sea when Paddy and Graham haven't asked yet and Graham still needs paying for the cards. The coast gets its fields and the crown keeps its feet.
Eight a square, done. Both squares go in the ground, and the coast keeps its feet as well, Silke. That's one grain left in my purse, so nobody at this table should be afraid of me this year.
Province 5 buys two squares of sea, N26 and N27, for 40: Reina pays 24 and the crown 16, 8 a square. Reina has 1 grain left; the crown's reserve is 24, with Graham's salary of 5 still to pay.

Storyteller's tip: a square bought this year starts yielding with next year's harvest and pays for itself in a year. Your board card shows how many you need to break even, now and after the next card. A player in debt can't buy any.

Three squares for the south-east, Silke. That's forty-two from me and six a square from the crown, and I know what's left in your chest after Graham's paid, so I'm not asking for Reina's eight. Three hundred million mouths won't eat pots, and I'd rather owe nobody than sit on grain while my paddies go hungry.

Five a square, Paddy, as I offered at the start. You can cover forty-five and still have grain in your pocket, and Reina couldn't. Once Graham's paid there's barely a handful left in the chest, and he hasn't asked for his share yet. I won't leave the south centre with nothing just to give the south-east one more grain a square.
At 6 a square for Paddy's three squares the crown would have kept 6 (1 after Graham's salary), so Graham's squares could still have had a crown share.
Five a square it is, Silke, and fair enough. Graham's got to eat as well. Three squares go into the south-east, and I'll be back to four and a half grain, same as when I started out.
Province 6 buys three squares of sea, R25, R26 and S26, for 60: Paddy pays 45 and the crown 15, 5 a square. Paddy has 4.5 left; the crown's reserve is 9, with Graham's salary of 5 still to pay.

Storyteller's tip: a square bought this year starts yielding with next year's harvest and pays for itself in a year. Your board card shows how many you need to break even, now and after the next card. A player in debt can't buy any.

Four squares for the south centre, Silke. One a square from the crown, four in all, and that still leaves your chest enough for my five. I've done the sums. I don't need your eight, and I'm not leaving you short to pay me.

Province 7 buys four squares of the Warlord's land, T14 to T17, for 80: Graham pays 76 and the crown 4, 1 a square. Thirteen squares bought this year in all. Grain: Silke (the crown) 5, Reina 1, Paddy 4.5, Graham 27.5.
The auctions. Paddy holds only one type beside the board, so his last Bamboo Brush goes up, at a minimum he names in his bids. Reina and Graham have nothing left in stock. The Emperor doesn't bid.

Storyteller's tip: three quarters of every auction price goes to the Harvest Pile, not the seller, and every grain spent at auction is a grain not spent on land. Think ahead about what a bid costs your province next year, and feel free to say it out loud.
One grain in my purse and the minimum is two, so the brush is safe from me this year, Paddy. Keep it on your shelf if nobody bids. I'll be good for it once the coast fields come in.

Storyteller's tip: three quarters of every auction price goes to the Harvest Pile, not the seller, and every grain spent at auction is a grain not spent on land. Think ahead about what a bid costs your province next year, and feel free to say it out loud.
Two grain, and not a grain more, so it's open to anybody who wants it this year. If nobody does, Reina, it'll be on my shelf waiting for you once the coast comes in.

Storyteller's tip: three quarters of every auction price goes to the Harvest Pile, not the seller, and every grain spent at auction is a grain not spent on land. Think ahead about what a bid costs your province next year, and feel free to say it out loud.

Pass. I've got a brush, and I know what it looks like when someone buys a second one just to keep it from somebody. I won't do that. Paddy, the piece I'm waiting on is your Jar. I stood aside for your Customs House, and when you're ready to talk about that Jar, I'll be the one at this table with grain.

Paddy's Bamboo Brush opens at 2 and nobody bids, so it stays beside the board and must go up again next year at 2. Silke pays Graham 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 6: Silke (the crown) 0, Reina 1, Paddy 4.5, Graham 32.5. Thirteen squares of new land were bought this year (Province 1 four, 5 two, 6 three, 7 four), each yielding 20 from next year. Nobody is in debt. Still owed: the Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160). Still beside the board: Paddy 1 Bamboo Brush.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile. Your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares.

Bad Harvest. "The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame." Every province collects a bad harvest. The counter stays at three hundred million, so that's times three. Read your bad-year row at x3 and count it before you spend anything you don't have.

Graham reads Bad Harvest: a bad harvest for every province, no disasters, the population holds at 300 million (x3). This year's incomes: Silke (the crown) -30, Reina -30, Paddy -10, Graham +30. Before the harvest is paid, each player may give, lend or trade.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile. Your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares.

Well. The ox went lame on all of us except Graham. The crown has nothing in the chest because every grain went into the ground last year, just as I promised. Graham, lend the crown thirty and you get thirty-five back from the first good harvest, before a single brick goes on the Wall. A crown in debt can't put a grain into anyone's land, and next year we'll all want those squares. Reina, Paddy, hold onto what you have. Nobody here is going to starve this year.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile. Your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares.

Graham, you're the only one at this table with a harvest this year, so I'll say it plainly. Lend me twenty-nine and I'll pay you back thirty-four, and you have my word in front of everyone that I won't bid against you for anything you want next year. You can carry the crown and the coast both: after your thirty comes in you'll have sixty-two and a half. Silke, I'm not trying to take your loan away from you. I just don't want to be the first person at this table to go into debt.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile. Your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares.

Graham, I'm short five and a half this year, and I'd rather ask you out loud than lose my pots to the Harvest Pile at two apiece. Lend me six and you'll have seven back from my first harvest before I spend a grain on anything else. It's the smallest ask at the table, and you know I paid what I owed on the Customs House.

Paddy, you asked me for six. I'll give you twelve, outright, for the Jar. That covers your harvest, you keep your other pots, and nothing goes to the Pile at two. Silke, I'll lend the crown twenty for twenty-five back, which is what I can spare. Reina, I'm sorry. I can't carry the whole coast, and I've already said where my grain is going.
Graham lends the crown 20 before the harvest, repaid 25 from the first good year's tax: Graham 12.5, the crown 20. He declines Reina's request and offers Paddy 12 for the Dragon Jar.

Graham, that Jar cost me more than any field I ever planted, and twelve's a thin price for the piece that finishes your set. Make it twelve now and six more when your harvest comes in, and you'll still have the twenty to change seats. If twelve is truly all you've got in you, I'll shake on twelve anyway, because I'd rather it went to you than to the Pile at two.

Graham pays Paddy 12 for the Dragon Jar, which moves from R22 to Q18: Graham's Wheat set is complete. Paddy's ask of 6 more after the harvest is open. Reina sells the Vase and the Land Deed Scroll back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each; they go into the pile's own stock, auctioned this year after the provinces' lots. The harvest: the crown -10 and Reina -25, both in debt; Paddy 6.5; Graham 30.5.

Paddy, you said you'd shake on twelve, and you meant it. That's why you get the other six. Here. And I'm staying where I am. Province 7 is the best farm on this board, and I'm not trading it for anybody's debt.
Graham pays Paddy the 6 more, 18 for the Jar in all, and stays the Wheat Peasant with his set on the board: Graham 24.5, Paddy 12.5.
Paddy's Bamboo Brush goes up at auction this year, Year 7, at 2.

The crown is in debt (-10). The tax is collected before the works and new land, and it pays the debt first: at 40% (12) the crown comes out at +2, and once its grain is back above zero it may pay a share of a work or of a square this year. Graham's loan of 20, repaid 25 from the first good year's tax, is the crown's to repay when it chooses.

Graham, you'll get your twenty-five back in the first good year, exactly as agreed. But a man who can pay eighteen for a Jar in a rotten harvest can pay fifteen in tax. That's fifty percent, and since you're the only one with a harvest, you're the only one who owes it. It clears the crown's debt and leaves five for the land. Paddy, the first square anyone buys this year gets five from the throne. Reina, get out of debt and I'll be back at your side. Nobody builds this year, because nobody can afford to.

Silke taxes at 50%: Paddy collects 15 from Graham on Province 7's +30, the only positive income. The crown goes from -10 to 5, out of debt. No work is built. The crown offers 5 on the first square any province buys this year and 1 on each after. Reina is in debt and can't buy land.
A Wheat set can't take the throne: at this table only the Silk Peasant may, with a Silk set. Graham's set lets him replace Reina or Paddy.

Thank you, Silke, and I mean it, but even with your five a square's fifteen to me, and I've only twelve and a half. I'm not going into debt for land, so I'll hold what I've got and come back for a square when I can pay my own share of it. And Graham, thank you for the six. You didn't have to give it.

Fifteen from the only harvest at this table, a year after I paid seventy-six to plant the crown's fields. I've written it down, Silke. No land for me this year. Nine and a half doesn't make a square, and I don't buy what I can't pay for.
Graham's 76 in Year 6 bought Province 7's own squares, T14 to T17; the crown paid 4 of that 80.

No new land this year: Paddy and Graham decline, Reina is in debt; thirteen squares. The auctions: Paddy's Bamboo Brush opens at 2 (unsold last year), then the Harvest Pile's Vase and Land Deed Scroll, minimum 2 each. Reina, in debt, can't bid; the Emperor doesn't.
Three times I've reached for that Vase. I'll put a couple of grain on it this time and no more, because without the Jar it's only a pretty pot, and I'm not paying over the odds for a pretty pot.
I'm passing on all three. I've got my set, and every grain I spend at auction is three-quarters gone to the Pile. Paddy, the Vase is yours to take if you want it.
Two grain for the Vase, after all that. Thank you for standing aside, Graham. It's going where the Jar used to sit, so I'll see that empty spot every morning.

The auctions: Paddy's Brush unsold at 2 (up again next year at 2); Paddy takes the Harvest Pile's Vase for 2 and puts it on R22; the pile's Land Deed Scroll unsold at 2 (up again next year). Silke pays Graham 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 7: Silke (the crown) 0, owing Graham 25 on his loan; Reina -25, in debt; Paddy 10.5; Graham 14.5. No land and no works this year: thirteen squares; 320 still owed. Beside the board: Paddy 1 Bamboo Brush; the Harvest Pile 1 Land Deed Scroll.

The Emperor's Share. "The Emperor would like to remind you who paid for the ditch." Average harvest everywhere, three hundred million, so read the x3 row. Every province with a Public Works gives the Emperor half of what it adds this round. I'll remind the table that I paid twenty of that ditch myself.

Graham reads The Emperor's Share: an average harvest for every province, x3. Only Province 7's Reservoir is a work outside the crown's province, so after the harvest Graham pays Silke 10, half its 20. This year's incomes: Silke -5, Reina -5, Paddy +15, Graham +55. Before the harvest, each player may give, lend or trade.

Graham, you wrote it down, so write this down too. The ten you send the crown for that Reservoir goes back into your fields this year, ten a square, and Paddy gets the same. Reina, I can't hand you grain I haven't got, but the coast is still my first canal when the chest can carry it. This is an ordinary year, and I mean to tax it like one.

Graham, last year you told me you couldn't carry the whole coast, and you were right, you couldn't. This year you'll clear fifty-nine after the Emperor's Share. Thirty of that gets me out of the hole, and I pay back thirty-six the first year the coast makes money. I've got nothing left to sell, so all I can offer is my word and my voice: you've heard me keep my word once already, and until you're paid back I side with you on every tax rate. Silke, if he does it, I want your share on my first square, the way you promised Paddy his.

Graham, you've told the whole table you're staying on the best farm in China, so the Jar's no use to you except sitting on a shelf. I'll give you twenty for it after the harvest, two more than you paid, and in grain I've actually got. Reina, I'm sorry, I've nothing to spare for the coast, but I won't vote you down on the tax either.
The harvest is paid: Reina -30, in debt; Paddy 25.5; Graham 69.5, then he pays Silke the Emperor's Share, 10, half his Reservoir's 20: Graham 59.5, the crown 5.

Reina, I'm sorry. Thirty grain in exchange for "the first year the coast makes money" is a promise with no date on it, and the tax hasn't been called yet. Paddy, I paid eighteen for that Jar in the worst year we've had, and twenty won't buy it back. A set on my shelf is worth more to me than two grain.
Graham declines Reina's loan and Paddy's offer for the Jar, and stays the Wheat Peasant.
Paddy holds the Vase, a Land Deed Scroll and the Customs House: the Dragon Jar alone would complete his Rice set.

Fifty percent. That's thirty-five out of a table that just paid Graham fifty-five, and every grain of it goes back into the ground. One square for the north so the throne stops eating its own reserve, and ten a square on your first two, Paddy, Graham, just as I said. Reina, once you're clear of debt, the coast canal is the first stone I lay.

Silke taxes at 50%: Paddy collects 35 (Paddy 7.5 on +15, Graham 27.5 on +55). The crown 5 to 40. No work is built. Province 1 buys E23 for 20, paid by the crown: the crown 20. The crown offers 10 a square on the first two squares Paddy or Graham buy this year, 1 a square after. Reina is in debt and can't buy land.
My mistake, I counted the tax wrong. Just the one square, then, R27, ten from me and ten from the crown. That leaves the crown's other ten for Graham's first square, which is only fair.
Province 6 buys R27: Paddy pays 10 and the crown 10. Paddy 8, the crown 10.
One square, T18. Ten from me and ten from the crown, as promised. Thank you, Paddy, for leaving it there. That's twenty a year for ten of mine, and even I can't argue with those numbers.
Province 7 buys T18: Graham pays 10 and the crown 10. Graham 22, the crown 0. Sixteen squares now.
The auctions: Paddy's Bamboo Brush must open at 2 (unsold last year), then the Harvest Pile's Land Deed Scroll at 2. Reina is in debt and can't bid; the Emperor doesn't.
I've already got a Scroll, so I'm passing on this one. Reina, I'd keep it back for you if I could, but the rules won't let me. The Brush is still on my shelf for whoever wants it.
I'm passing on both. I have twenty-two, and twenty of it is spoken for.
Nobody bids: Paddy's Brush and the pile's Land Deed Scroll stay unsold, both up again next year at 2.

Graham, the chest is empty because every grain went into your field, Paddy's and mine. I won't put the crown into debt to pay you with grain I'd only have to borrow back. Your five goes on the slate, so that's thirty owed, and it's the first thing paid out of next year's tax. Same jobs as before. Nobody at this table has done them badly.

Silke defers Graham's 5 for the I Ching: the crown now owes Graham 30, to be paid first from next year's tax. The jobs stay the same for Year 9. End of Year 8: Silke (the crown) 0, owing Graham 30; Reina -30, in debt; Paddy 8; Graham 22. Sixteen squares (Province 1 five, 5 two, 6 four, 7 five). No works built in Years 7 and 8; the Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160) are still owed. Graham holds the Wheat set; Paddy needs only the Jar; Reina holds nothing. Beside the board: Paddy 1 Bamboo Brush; the Harvest Pile 1 Land Deed Scroll.
